title: Dogen's Genjokoan, part two
hook: read the moon in a dewdrop, and the fish in the water
tomorrow: why would a teacher with followers say he had not one student?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the opening of Dogen's Genjokoan: flowers fall amid our longing, weeds spread amid our dislike, and practice happens right there. The way is here. Today, the same essay, and a drop of water.
screen: `THE WAY IS HERE.` → `A DROP OF WATER.`

segments.voice: Something gets sent today: an application, a résumé, a message that took a week to write. The button gets pressed, and suddenly the thing that filled the whole week looks very small against the world it's going out into. Dogen answers that feeling with a drop of water. In paraphrase from the Genjokoan: the whole moon and the whole sky are reflected in a single dewdrop on the grass.
screen: `THE BUTTON GETS PRESSED.` → `SUDDENLY IT LOOKS SMALL.` → `THE WHOLE MOON IN ONE DEWDROP.`

segments.voice: Here's the passage around it, in paraphrase. Awakening is like the moon reflected in water. The moon doesn't get wet, and the water isn't broken. Its light is wide and great, and yet it rests even in a tiny puddle. The whole moon, the whole sky, in one dewdrop. Notice what Dogen doesn't say. He doesn't say the dewdrop is secretly big. It stays a dewdrop. And he doesn't say the moon gets smaller to fit. The whole thing is there, in the small thing, without either one being damaged. Then he gives a second picture. A fish swims in water, and however far it swims, the water has no end. A bird flies in the sky, and however far it flies, the sky has no end. Yet no fish has ever left the water, no bird the sky. They use all of it, wherever they are. That's Dogen's answer to the small feeling. A life, a week of work, one drawing, isn't a scrap of the whole that might not count. It's a dewdrop, and the whole moon is in it. The way isn't measured by size. It's met, the essay says, right where you stand, the way a fish meets the water it's in.
screen: `THE MOON DOESN'T GET WET.` · `A SMALL DROP, A WHOLE MOON.` · `THE FISH NEVER LEAVES THE WATER.` · `NOT MEASURED BY SIZE.` · then, large: `THE MOON IN A DEWDROP.`

segments.voice: Pour a little water into a glass or a bowl, or find a drop on a window or a leaf. Look into it until you find light in it: a lamp, the window, the sky. Rest your eyes there and notice how much fits in so little, until the bell.
Dogen's Genjokoan, part two: the moon reflected whole in a dewdrop, and the fish that never leaves the water. Small things hold whole things.
Here is the line: the moon in a dewdrop, whole, and nothing broken. Six of eleven in this block.

howItsDone: Soto Zen teachers often turn to the Genjokoan's moon-in-water and fish-and-bird passages in talks; students study the essay slowly, a passage at a time.

fork.setup: your friend volunteers one hour a week at a food bank and says it's 'basically nothing' next to the world's hunger. what does the dewdrop say?

fork.reveal: the dewdrop stays a dewdrop, and the whole moon is in it. Dogen's measure isn't size.

original.note: Japanese: genjō, what is appearing now; kōan, a case to be worked through; Dogen's essay.

what a scholar hears: the Genjōkōan's moon-in-water simile (the moon not wet, the water not broken) and the fish-and-bird passage, read together as practice-realization.
